pharm: Fixed-combination antibacterial pairing sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim in a 5:1 ratio; produces sequential blockade of bacterial folate synthesis with synergistic, broadly bactericidal activity.
quick: 1 DS tablet (800/160 mg) PO q12h for most infections
Take with a full glass of water; food optional, maintain hydration
Avoid, esp. 1st trimester & near term (neural tube defects, kernicterus)
Avoid in ill/premature/jaundiced/G6PD-deficient infants; otherwise caution
Reduce dose 50% if CrCl 15-30; avoid/contraindicated if CrCl <15
Avoid; rare disulfiram-like reaction and additive hepatotoxicity

summary: Co-trimoxazole is a fixed combination of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim (5:1) that blocks two sequential steps of bacterial folate synthesis, giving synergistic activity against many Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms and Pneumocystis jirovecii. Standard formulations are single-strength (400/80 mg) and double-strength/DS (800/160 mg) tablets, plus oral suspension and IV. Mainstays of use are urinary tract infections and the treatment and prophylaxis of Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP). Major safety concerns are severe cutaneous reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis), blood dyscrasias, hyperkalemia (especially at high doses, in renal impairment, or with ACE inhibitors/ARBs/potassium-sparing agents), and hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Dose adjustment is required for moderate renal impairment, and it is contraindicated in severe renal or hepatic disease, megaloblastic anemia from folate deficiency, pregnancy near term, and infants under 2 months.
indications: Urinary tract infections (susceptible E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Proteus species)
Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCP) pneumonia - prophylaxis (primary and secondary)
Acute exacerbations of chronic bronchitis in adults (susceptible strains)
Acute otitis media in children (susceptible S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae)
Enteritis caused by susceptible Shigella flexneri and Shigella sonnei (shigellosis)
Traveler's diarrhea due to susceptible enterotoxigenic E. coli
Other off-label uses: skin and soft-tissue infections incl. MRSA, toxoplasmosis, nocardiosis, Listeria, Stenotrophomonas

dosage.n: UTI/bronchitis 10-14 days; shigellosis 5 days; equivalent to 2 single-strength tablets or 20 mL suspension q12h

dosage.d: 8 mg/kg TMP + 40 mg/kg SMX per day
dosage.n: UTI/otitis 10 days; shigellosis 5 days; not for infants <2 months
Duration 14-21 days; dose by trimethoprim component; ensure hydration
Single-strength 400/80 mg daily is an alternative; continue per immune status
Total daily TMP dose should not exceed 320 mg

dosage.d: Give 50% of the usual recommended dose

dosage.n: Avoid; contraindicated in severe renal insufficiency where renal function cannot be monitored

admin: Take oral doses with a full glass (8 oz) of water
Maintain adequate fluid intake throughout therapy to prevent crystalluria and stone formation
May be taken with or without food; food can reduce GI upset
Shake oral suspension well before measuring each dose
IV: dilute each 5 mL in 125 mL of 5% dextrose and infuse over 60-90 minutes; do not give rapid or bolus injection; avoid mixing with other drugs or solutions
Complete the full prescribed course even if feeling better
moa: Sequential blockade of the bacterial folic acid pathway: sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase (competing with para-aminobenzoic acid to block dihydrofolic acid formation), while trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (blocking conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate). This two-step inhibition of folate synthesis is synergistic and bactericidal, depriving bacteria of the reduced folates needed for nucleic acid and protein synthesis; selectivity arises from the far greater affinity of trimethoprim for bacterial than human dihydrofolate reductase.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to trimethoprim, sulfamethoxazole, or any sulfonamide
History of drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia with sulfonamides/trimethoprim
Documented megaloblastic anemia due to folate deficiency
Marked hepatic damage / severe hepatic insufficiency
Severe renal insufficiency when renal function cannot be monitored (CrCl <15 mL/min)
Pregnancy at term and during the period of labor/delivery
Infants younger than 2 months of age
relative: Pregnancy (especially first trimester) - neural tube defect risk
Folate deficiency states (elderly, malnourished, alcoholism, anticonvulsant or malabsorption-associated)
Hypothyroidism, severe allergy, or bronchial asthma
monitor: Complete blood count during prolonged or high-dose therapy
Skin - discontinue at first appearance of rash

preg: Avoid, particularly in the first trimester (folate antagonism associated with neural tube and other defects) and near term (risk of neonatal kernicterus from bilirubin displacement). Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit clearly outweighs the risk; supplement with folic acid if used. Contraindicated at term/during labor and delivery.
lact: Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim are excreted in breast milk. Avoid in mothers nursing ill, premature, stressed, jaundiced, or G6PD-deficient infants because of the risk of kernicterus and hemolysis; otherwise use with caution in healthy term infants. Contraindicated in infants younger than 2 months.
renal: Requires dose adjustment. For CrCl 15-30 mL/min, give half the usual dose. For CrCl below 15 mL/min, use is not recommended/contraindicated. Maintain hydration; risk of crystalluria and accumulation of both components plus hyperkalemia rises with renal impairment. Monitor renal function and potassium.
hepatic: Contraindicated in marked hepatic parenchymal damage. Use with caution in lesser hepatic impairment; rare cases of fulminant hepatic necrosis and cholestatic jaundice have occurred. Discontinue if signs of hepatic injury develop.

major: Warfarin and other coumarin anticoagulants - inhibits metabolism and prolongs INR/bleeding; monitor closely and reduce anticoagulant dose
Methotrexate - displaces from protein binding and additive antifolate effect, increasing toxicity (myelosuppression); avoid concurrent use
ACE inhibitors / ARBs / potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone) - additive risk of severe, sometimes fatal hyperkalemia
Dofetilide - trimethoprim raises dofetilide levels, increasing risk of QT prolongation/torsades (contraindicated)
Phenytoin - decreased clearance and increased phenytoin levels/effect
moderate: Digoxin - increased serum digoxin concentrations, especially in the elderly
Cyclosporine - increased nephrotoxicity and decreased cyclosporine levels (renal transplant)
Pyrimethamine (>25 mg/week) - increased risk of megaloblastic anemia
Diuretics (thiazides, in the elderly) - increased incidence of thrombocytopenia with purpura
Amantadine, memantine, dapsone - increased levels of both drugs
minor: Procainamide - increased levels via reduced renal clearance
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; take with a full glass of water and maintain fluid intake. Avoid excessive potassium-rich salt substitutes.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; rare disulfiram-like (flushing) reactions and additive hepatotoxicity have been reported.
interactions.diagnostics: Trimethoprim interferes with the Jaffe alkaline picrate creatinine assay, falsely raising measured serum creatinine by ~10% (no true loss of renal function); it can also interfere with serum methotrexate assays using competitive binding protein. May produce false-positive urine glucose tests.

serious: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions - Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)
Blood dyscrasias - agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, thrombocytopenia, megaloblastic anemia, neutropenia, hemolytic anemia
Hyperkalemia (dose-related; worse with renal impairment or K-raising drugs)
Fulminant hepatic necrosis and cholestatic jaundice
Acute kidney injury, interstitial nephritis, crystalluria
rare: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
emergency: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / toxic epidermal necrolysis (any spreading rash, blistering, mucosal lesions, skin peeling)
Agranulocytosis or severe pancytopenia (fever, sore throat, bleeding)

monitoring: Complete blood count (CBC) periodically, especially with prolonged or high-dose therapy; discontinue if a significant reduction in any formed blood element occurs
Serum potassium, particularly with high doses, renal impairment, or concomitant ACEi/ARB/K-sparing drugs
Renal function (serum creatinine, BUN) and urinalysis; remember trimethoprim falsely elevates Jaffe creatinine
Serum sodium and glucose in at-risk patients
Vigilance for skin rash - stop the drug at the first sign
INR in patients on warfarin; phenytoin and digoxin levels where co-administered
counsel: Stop the medicine and seek medical care immediately if you develop any rash, blistering, peeling skin, mouth or eye sores, or fever - these can signal a serious skin reaction
Report sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers, pallor, unusual bruising or bleeding (possible blood problems)
Drink plenty of fluids while taking this medicine to protect your kidneys and prevent stones
It can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight - use sunscreen and protective clothing and avoid prolonged sun exposure
Take with a full glass of water and complete the entire course as directed
Tell your clinician about blood thinners, diabetes medicines, blood pressure medicines (ACE inhibitors/ARBs), potassium supplements, and any history of sulfa allergy or G6PD deficiency
pk: Antibacterial effect within hours; clinical UTI response over 1-3 days
Plasma peak ~1-4 hours after oral dose
Sulfamethoxazole ~10 hours; trimethoprim ~8-10 hours (both prolonged in renal impairment)
Supports every-12-hour dosing for most infections
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect tablets and suspension from light; do not refrigerate IV concentrate
pearls: Discontinue immediately at the first appearance of skin rash - co-trimoxazole is a leading cause of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN); never re-challenge after a severe reaction
Can cause serious blood dyscrasias (agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, thrombocytopenia, megaloblastic anemia) - monitor CBC and stop if counts fall
Hyperkalemia is dose-related and especially dangerous with high PCP-treatment doses, renal impairment, or combined with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or potassium-sparing diuretics - check serum potassium
May trigger acute hemolytic anemia in G6PD-deficient patients - use with caution and consider screening in at-risk populations
Trimethoprim blocks tubular creatinine secretion and interferes with the Jaffe assay, causing a benign ~10% rise in measured serum creatinine without true loss of renal function
Dose PCP treatment by the trimethoprim component (15-20 mg/kg/day) divided q6-8h; adjunctive corticosteroids are indicated for moderate-severe PCP in HIV
Markedly potentiates warfarin (raises INR) and sulfonylureas (hypoglycemia), and raises phenytoin and digoxin levels
Maintain hydration to avoid crystalluria; avoid in folate-deficient states given antifolate mechanism
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and resume the regular schedule. Do not take two doses at once or a double dose to make up. For PCP treatment, contact the prescriber if doses are missed, as therapeutic levels must be maintained.
overdose: Signs of acute overdose include nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, confusion, and bone marrow depression with prolonged or massive ingestion. Management: induce emesis or gastric lavage if recent; ensure adequate fluid intake and urine output; acidify urine to enhance sulfamethoxazole elimination. Monitor CBC, serum potassium, and electrolytes. Hemodialysis is only moderately effective (peritoneal dialysis is not). Leucovorin (folinic acid) 5-15 mg/day reverses trimethoprim-induced bone marrow suppression/megaloblastic effects. Provide supportive care.
